name: Priya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and capper on a bottling line at a soft drinks plant, mostly lemonade and orange in two-litre bottles. I set the fill levels, swap the cap hoppers, clean the nozzles at changeover, and watch the reject camera so I can catch problems before the supervisor does. We do twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off. The four off are the best part, honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life around those shifts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Dan, he's an electrician, self-employed, so his money goes up and down. We're saving for a house deposit, and we've got about four months of bills put aside on top. On my days off I do a pottery class at the community centre, which is the opposite of my job, slow and messy. I use AI on my phone sometimes, mostly to plan meals or check the wording of an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, then, and probably make a joke about all the money spent on it. At work we'd have a laugh about the robot that was supposed to replace us. I don't post much, maybe a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we can buy the house without worrying. My job carries on, Dan's carries on. Honestly that's the best news for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead and put an offer in on a house in the next year, probably a small terrace near Dan's mum. I'd keep going on my shifts as normal. Maybe I'd ask about the team leader role when it comes up, since there'd be no big change to wait for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, mostly, like someone's taken a weight off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What routine tasks on your line do you think AI might take over, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The changeovers, maybe. Right now swapping from two-litre to half-litre bottles takes me forty minutes with a checklist and a spanner, and AI might set some of it up faster. I'd still be the one watching the camera and catching a bad cap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the team leader role. Would you go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'm good with the people on my shift and I know the line. It'd be about thirty more a week, not much, but it'd help with the mortgage.

S0.say: I'd say that's that, then, and joke about all the money spent on it. At work we'd laugh about the robot that was supposed to replace us, and I might post a meme.
S0.think: It means we can buy the house without worrying, with both my job and Dan's carrying on. That's the best possible news for us.
S0.do: Puts an offer in on a small terrace near Dan's mum within the year and carries on her shifts. Applies for the team leader role, worth about 30 more a week.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a weight lifted.
S0.quote: At work we'd have a laugh about the robot that was supposed to replace us.
S0.fieldNote: Priya measures every picture against one goal: buying a house with Dan. In the calm picture that goal goes ahead, and she'd even reach for a promotion. Her tone is practical and friendly, not ideological.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to get ready. The firms that change well will keep people, the ones that don't will close anyway. I'd tell people on my shift to get any training going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the filler already pretty much runs itself, it's me who catches the problems. If a camera and AI catch the problems, there's not much left of my job. I'd probably last a while, but on a smaller crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what the company offers, then sign up for whatever line technician training they're running, once a couple of the others have tried it. We'd hold off on the house for maybe six months. I'd move a bit more into savings, about a hundred and fifty extra a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be watching the noticeboard more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to try the training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last new thing they brought in, a scheduling app, was gone in three months. I'd rather not spend my days off on a course for something that disappears. Once I see it sticking, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would delaying the house cause any friction with Dan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. He thinks people will always need electricians. But his work is lumpy, and if mine goes too, the mortgage would be on us both. I'd rather be sure.

S1.say: I'd say it's sensible to get ready, because firms that change well keep people and the rest close anyway. I'd tell people on my shift to take any training going.
S1.think: The filler mostly runs itself and I'm the one catching problems, so if a camera and AI do that, there's not much left. I'd likely last a while on a smaller crew.
S1.do: Waits a few months, then joins company line technician training once colleagues have tried it. Delays the house purchase about six months and saves an extra 150 a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching the noticeboard more than she'd like.
S1.quote: If a camera and AI catch the problems, there's not much left of my job.
S1.fieldNote: Priya sees exactly which part of her job is at risk: the watching and catching. She'd adapt once she sees a change sticking, shaped by a short-lived scheduling app. Dan's irregular income makes her more careful about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a real plan from the government, now, not after. Some kind of help for people while things shake out. I'd be saying it in our family chat more than anywhere public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the bottling line would be robots and cameras within a year or two, and I'd be out. Dan's work might hold a bit longer, but if robots can wire houses too, not for long. The house would be off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house, full stop, and keep the deposit as a safety net, which together with savings would give us maybe a year. I'd cut the pottery class and the takeaways. I'd look straight away for any job that still needs a person, maybe at the care home where my aunt works, even though I'd have no idea how long that would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's tilting and I can't find the rail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about the house. What does giving it up mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want it eventually. But you don't sign a twenty-five-year mortgage when you can't see two years ahead. That'd be daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in the very first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to Dan about where we'd live cheapest. Maybe with his mum for a while. And go through every bill and cancel the ones we don't need, the gym, the streaming, the second phone line he uses for work.

S2.say: I'd say this needs a real plan from the government now, with help for people while things shake out. I'd say it in our family chat more than anywhere public.
S2.think: The bottling line would be robots and cameras within a year or two, and I'd be out. Dan's work might hold a bit longer, but the house would be off.
S2.do: Cancels the house plan and keeps the deposit as a safety net, stretching their cushion to about a year. Cuts her pottery class and takeaways, considers living with Dan's mum, and looks immediately for other work, such as at her aunt's care home.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the floor is tilting and she can't find the rail.
S2.quote: But you don't sign a twenty-five-year mortgage when you can't see two years ahead.
S2.fieldNote: The house plan is the first casualty and Priya says so plainly. The deposit fund gives her more runway than her savings alone suggest. Her move toward care work is immediate but she admits she can't tell how long it would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort this if people start now. Courses, help switching, that kind of thing. I'd say get trained while you can, same as in the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd maybe get three years on the line, then the same end. The difference is I could see it coming. I'd want to use those years for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time I wouldn't wait to see what others do. I'd start a technician course in the first year, and also look into nursing assistant training as a backup. We'd keep the deposit untouched for two years and decide on the house then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like revising for an exam you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the steady picture you'd wait for others. Why not this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one there was time to be choosy. With five years, waiting six months is a tenth of it gone. I'd rather start and switch than sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide the house question at the two-year mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If by then it looks like real jobs are still out there, we'd buy something smaller than we wanted. If not, we'd rent and keep the money. I'd be fine with either, as long as we're not stuck.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to sort this if people start now, with courses and help switching. I'd tell people to get trained while they can.
S3.think: I'd maybe get three more years on the line before the same end, but I'd see it coming. I'd want to use those years for something.
S3.do: Starts a technician course in year one and looks into nursing assistant training as a backup. Keeps the deposit untouched for two years before deciding on the house.
S3.feel: Anxious but organised, like revising for an exam she knows is coming.
S3.quote: With five years, waiting six months is a tenth of it gone.
S3.fieldNote: Priya drops her usual wait-for-proof habit once the deadline is clear, and does the maths aloud. She hedges by pursuing two paths at once. The house decision is postponed rather than abandoned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and the sensible thing is to plan now. Companies and the government should help people move into new work gradually. I'd probably say it in a fairly boring way, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly fine. I'd be thirty-seven at the end, and I could do a nursing assistant course part time and still have time to change again. The house we'd buy, because ten years of paying a mortgage is ten years of owning more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house in the next year or so. I'd keep working the line for a couple of years, then start a care or nursing course around year three. I'd keep saving a little, maybe a hundred a month on top of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly OK. It's far enough away that I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work is hands-on. Do you worry robots would reach that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My aunt does it and she says the machines help with lifting but nobody wants a robot to talk to at three in the morning. I might be wrong, though, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, with ten years to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the team leader job. If I'm planning to leave in three years anyway, the extra stress might not be worth thirty quid a week. I'd rather put the energy into the course.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and the sensible thing is to plan now, with companies and government helping people move gradually. I'd say it in a fairly boring way.
S4.think: It's mostly fine for me, because at thirty-seven I could retrain part time and still change again. We'd buy the house, since ten years of mortgage means owning more of it.
S4.do: Buys the house within about a year and keeps working the line for a couple of years. Starts a care or nursing course around year three and saves about 100 a month on top of the mortgage.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly OK, far enough off to plan around.
S4.quote: Nobody wants a robot to talk to at three in the morning.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Priya go ahead with the house and plan a calm move into care. She draws on her aunt's experience but admits she might be wrong. She'd also give up on the team leader role to focus her energy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. The house would be gone, I'd be out of work, and Dan's work would be shaky too. What would help is some kind of wage support for a year while people switch, and short, paid courses for jobs that actually exist, not vague ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about Dan. People ask about my job, but in our house it's both of us. If I could know his work was safe for five years, I'd feel completely different about mine.

headlineQuote: If I could know his work was safe for five years, I'd feel completely different about mine.
portrait: Priya Petrov, 27, runs the filler and capper on a soft drinks bottling line and lives with her partner Dan, a self-employed electrician. Their shared goal of buying a house shapes how she reacts to every picture. She is practical and middle-of-the-road, uses AI now and then for small tasks, and normally waits to see a change stick before joining in. Calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, she becomes decisive once there's a clear deadline, retraining straight away with five years and buying the house before a move into care work with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because the house plan would collapse and both her job and Dan's would be in doubt.
whatWouldHelp: A year of wage support while people switch, and short, paid courses for jobs that actually exist.
